label: Person
name: István Werbőczy
summary:
István Werbőczy (c. 1458–1541) was a Hungarian legal theorist, statesman, and author of the Tripartitum — the codification of Hungarian customary law that remained the constitutional foundation of the Kingdom of Hungary for over three centuries and institutionalized the legal privileges of the Hungarian nobility.

Werbőczy compiled the Tripartitum Opus Iuris Consuetudinarii Inclyti Regni Hungariae (1517) — a comprehensive compilation of Hungarian constitutional custom — by royal commission. The work established the principle of the 'one and same liberty' of all Hungarian nobles (nobilitas una eademque), legally equalizing nobles regardless of wealth and creating the constitutional fiction of noble sovereignty over royal power. This legal framework — the 'noble democracy' — became the defining characteristic of Hungarian constitutionalism and shaped political culture well into the 19th century.

The Tripartitum also codified serfdom in its harshest form: following the Dózsa peasant revolt (1514), Werbőczy oversaw legislation permanently binding serfs to the land and stripping them of all legal rights. The law's passage just two years before the Ottoman catastrophe at Mohács (1526) meant that Hungarian society entered its 150-year partition under the Ottoman and Habsburg empires deeply divided between a legally privileged nobility and a dispossessed peasantry. Werbőczy himself fled to Turkish-controlled Buda, where he served as an Ottoman judicial official until his death in 1541 — a controversial end for the man who had defined Hungarian noble liberty.
